  built-in auditor, which may open eDiscovery alone, sees Compliance with eDiscovery where it saw Monitoring &
  troubleshooting with eDiscovery as its only row. Spam & virus filtering held fourteen pages on two subjects, the
  virus scanning overview its twelfth row under eleven spam pages: the three virus pages are Virus scanning now, after
  it, under a bug, the overview first, and the group is Spam filtering, whose description names the checks, the lists
  and the quarantine and no virus. The old heading is a search alias of both groups and every page keeps its key, so
  links, tours, Related links and automation ids arrive as before; the Allowed and blocked domains page's place in the
  null-sender card's text says Spam filtering in every language. At 760 by 520 the rail's last glyphs are below the
  fold, as the owner accepted (review findings F152 and F153, decision of 12 October 2026). `SidebarStructureTests`
  holds the two groups, their glyphs, their pages and the auditor's sidebar.

- **Changed: the two TLS pages are TLS certificates and TLS versions & ciphers.** The glossary says TLS in prose and
  SSL only for what is named so, and the two pages kept SSL in their titles until the page names were decided again:
  SSL certificates, and SSL/TLS, which was also the name of the connection security that encrypts from the first byte,
  so that a port's SSL/TLS and the page of that name read alike. By the owner's decision of 12 October 2026 they are
  TLS certificates and TLS versions & ciphers, in the sidebar, the breadcrumb, the page heading and every text that
  names them, in every language, and so are a port's TLS certificate box, the certificate list's failed read, the
  setup checklist's certificate items and the audit trail's word for a certificate; the old titles are search aliases,
  SSL/TLS stays the connection security's name, and the help opens the section of SettingsReasons.md now headed TLS
  versions & ciphers (review finding F301). `GlossaryTests` holds SSL to SSL/TLS and OpenSSL alone, and the two titles
  and their aliases.

- **Changed: the spam group's six allow and block lists are under a sub-heading, Lists.** Spam filtering was a run of
  flat rows in which nothing said which pages were lists: five ways to let a sender through and three to refuse one,
  spread over Spam exemptions, Blocked senders, Allow and block list, Greylisting exemptions, Greylisting bypass list
  and Allowed and blocked domains. They follow the checks and their block lists under the caption Lists now, in the
  sidebar and in the rail's flyout, in every language; the spam overview's "Which list do I need?" still tells them
  apart. The sub-heading is a caption at the pages' text column that neither the pointer nor the keyboard lands on, so
  the arrow keys go from the page above it to the page below, and a level-3 heading to a screen reader; it is not a
  level of the tree, so the breadcrumb, the palette and every link are as they were, and a role that cannot open the
  first list sees it over the first one it can (review finding F269; the Virus sub-heading the review also proposed is
  the Virus scanning group). `SidebarStructureTests` holds the run, the sub-heading's place and its row.

- **Changed: API & monitoring is Monitoring & alerts, and holds the alerts, the outbound webhooks and the SNMP agent;
  the Windows Event Log is on Logging, and ManageSieve is a tab of Protocols.** Logging held the Alerts & webhooks and
  SNMP tabs, which tell another system what happened, while its neighbour API & monitoring held the Windows Event Log,
  where the log goes, and the ManageSieve listener, a mail protocol; its Webhooks alias outranked the page that had
  the webhook settings, and nothing said where ManageSieve was but the Protocols page's Services card, which sent the
  reader to API & monitoring. The page is Monitoring & alerts now, in five tabs - REST API, Metrics, Alerts &
  webhooks, SNMP and Shutdown - with the same settings, words and warnings: the metrics listener's five warnings, the
  bearer token's and the HTTP Basic password's Generate and Remove the stored secret when saving, and every port and
  number held as typed to the server's range and refused on its field by a save. The Windows Event Log is a card of
  Logging's Logging tab, after syslog, and ManageSieve a tab of Protocols with the state of the STARTTLS it borrows a
  certificate for. A search for Alerts, Webhooks or SNMP opens Monitoring & alerts on the tab that holds it, Windows
  Event Log opens Logging and Sieve or ManageSieve the ManageSieve tab; the old title is a search alias, the page's
  key is unchanged, every sentence that named the page names it anew in every language, and the REST API's refusal on
  a page no longer offers to open the page it is on (review finding F273, the owner's decision of 12 October 2026).
  `PageSubjectsTests` holds the cards on their pages, their warnings and secrets, the aliases, the descriptions and
  the task that opens them; `SettingNumberRangeTests` holds the moved numbers to their ranges and the addresses to
  their width.

- **Changed: the limits every rule is held to are a Rule limits card on the Rules page.** They were the Rules tab of
  Delivery of e-mail - the rule loop limit, and the account-number pattern the sensitive-content condition looks for -
  one sidebar row from the Rules page, and the tab had to say where the rules were. The card is under the rules now,
  with its own Save rule limits, which Ctrl+S presses, and the pill that says whether what is on screen has reached
  the server; the page asks before it is left with an unsaved edit of the card, F5 and Refresh read the card again
  unless it holds one, the loop limit and the pattern, found by a search as settings, open the page on the card - the
  page itself, which the same search finds first, opens on its rules - and the account dialog's Rules tab, whose rules
  are the account's, has no card. Delivery of e-mail has no Rules tab, and the reasons document keeps the pattern's
  under Rules (review finding F273, the owner's decision of 12 October 2026). The card is the settings pages' own,
  shown on another page with no frame of its own, its Save captioned in the page's words so that its access key is
  free there in every language, and the REST API's notice, while the API cannot be used - as shipped, with its port
  0 - the card's first row, whose button carries no access key and is reached by Tab, where above the card its Alt+O was
  Remove criterion's too. `check-mnemonics.py` holds the Save and the notice to the page's keys in every language.
  `PageSubjectsTests` holds the card on the page, the page's questions to it and the frame it does not draw.

- **Changed: the PROXY protocol and XCLIENT are a card on the Incoming relays page.** Both let a named upstream - a
  load balancer, a TLS terminator, a Postfix relay - pass on the real client address, which is what the Incoming
  relays page is about, and they were a card of Server limits & expert settings. They are a Front-end proxies card
  under the relays now, with its own Save proxy settings, which Ctrl+S presses, its pill, the page's question before
  it is left with an unsaved edit, F5 reading the card again only while it holds none, and the same four settings,
  words and examples; Server limits & expert settings lists them among the settings that used to be on it, with the
  way to them, a search for PROXY protocol, HAProxy or XCLIENT opens Incoming relays, and so does the task "put a
  proxy in front of the server" (review finding F273, the owner's decision of 12 October 2026). The help on Incoming
  relays opens their reasons, under Incoming relays in the reasons document. `PageSubjectsTests` holds the card on the
  page and the signpost.

- **Changed: the mailbox migrations and the PST import are a card on the backup page, which is Backup, restore &
  migration.** The two settings the server keeps for them - how many connections every running migration may hold to
  one source host, and the folder PST files are copied into for import - were the Migrations tab of Advanced, a page
  named for nothing in particular, and bringing mail in from another server or an Outlook data file is the backup
  page's subject as much as a restore is. They are a Migrations card under the restore cards now, with the Control
  Deck's button the jobs are started from, its own Save migration settings in the card's footer, which Ctrl+S presses
  while the keyboard is in the card, its pill, the REST API's notice as the card's first row while the API cannot be
  used, its button without an access key, and the page's question before it is left with an unsaved edit of the card;
  Advanced has no Migrations tab, a search for Migrations or PST import opens the backup page, and so does the task
  "import a pst file". The page's old title, Backup & restore, is a search alias, and the setup checklist's backup
  folder, the update's no-backup reason and the documents name the page by its new one (review finding F273, the
  owner's decision of 12 October 2026). `PageSubjectsTests` holds the card on the page and Advanced without it.

- **Changed: a route written before the sidebar's moves still opens its page.** The documents and an administrator's
  notes name pages by their sidebar route, as *Maintenance → Backup & restore* or *Spam & virus filtering → Anti-virus
  settings*, and twenty-one of those routes changed with the moves above: the spam group's eleven pages and the three
  virus pages, the audit trail, journaling and eDiscovery, and the four pages that were called SSL certificates,
  SSL/TLS, API & monitoring and Backup & restore. Ctrl+K takes each old route, with the arrow or with ">", and offers
  its page first, as it does the classic Administrator's paths. `NavigationMapTests` holds every route, and
  `PageSubjectsTests` the search.

- **Changed: the server's own texts name the renamed pages.** The alert that a certificate is expiring or has expired
  tells the administrator to replace the file on the TLS certificates page, and the unattended update that could not
  put the previous release back names the backup destination that Backup, restore & migration sets, where both used
  the pages' old titles, which only a search alias still found.

- **Fixed: a Control Panel signed in to a server on another machine shows the server's hMailServer.ini [Settings]
  values on the settings pages that hold them beside the server's other settings, and saves them.** On Protocols,
  Delivery of e-mail, Logging, Monitoring & alerts, Advanced and the other pages of that kind, the switches, texts,
  choices and numbers kept under [Settings] were read and written only when hMailServer.ini was on this computer, so
  that a remote Control Panel showed each at its default as though it were the server's value, and a save left it
  unwritten and said it was saved. Among them were the rows this release moves onto those pages and onto Incoming
  relays, whose INI-only page had refused to show what it could not read: the metrics listener's bind address read
  127.0.0.1 on a server bound to 0.0.0.0, without the warning that /metrics answers 503 there, ManageSieve on every
  address was said to be kept on this machine, and PROXY and XCLIENT were off whatever the server had. They ask the
  server now, as the moved ports and secrets already did, and read the file only without a session; a value that falls
  back to the file is marked Not read and left alone by a save. The [Database] rows of Performance's Database
  connections card, which the server does not answer over COM, are the file's alone, and a Control Panel that cannot
  read the file marks them Not read. The INI-only pages, such as Server limits & expert settings, still say that they
  can be edited only on the server. `RemoteIniRowsTests` holds the rows to the rule, and the store to the server's
  values and writes with no file on this computer.

- **Fixed: Performance's Database connections card marks its hMailServer.ini [Database] settings Not read where this
  Control Panel cannot read the file, and a save leaves them alone.** The connections in the pool, the attempts to
  reach the database at start-up and the seconds between them are read from the file on this computer, as the server
  does not answer that section over COM. A Control Panel on another machine, and one on the server that was not run as
  administrator - the file is the administrators' alone from 6.3.6 - had no value to read, showed each at its default
  as a live, editable value, and on a save said that an edit of one was saved, where nothing was written. Each is
  marked Not read now, the card says at its top why, and how to see and change the three, and a save neither writes
  nor counts them. `RemoteIniRowsTests` holds the rows and the card to it, and the store to the default it answers for
  [Database] with no file on this computer and with a file this user may not read.

- **Fixed: the Quarantine page's search looked only through the five hundred most recent held messages (review
  finding F261).** It filtered the page COM had loaded, so an older message could not be found from the page at all,
  and the Control Deck's search, filtering the newest thousand, could not either. The server searches every held
  message now. Over COM `Quarantine.Search(Text, Offset, Count)` loads a page of the messages whose sender,
  recipients, subject or reason holds the text, newest first, which `Item` then indexes, and answers how many match in
  all. Over REST `GET /api/v1/quarantine` takes `q`, `offset` and `limit` and answers a page as an object - `query`,
  `held`, `total`, `offset`, `count` and `messages` - and without them is the bare array of the newest thousand it
  always was; `GET /api/v1/me/quarantine` takes the same for an account's own held mail and looks in the sender, the
  subject and the reason, never in the recipients, which say who else a message was for. The text is matched as it is
  written, in any case, on all four databases: each LIKE has a parameter of its own, in the order SQL Server binds them
  by position, with `%`, `_`, `[` and the escape character escaped; on MySQL and PostgreSQL the database lowers the
  text as it lowers the column, so that "ÜBERWEISUNG" finds "Überweisung" on PostgreSQL, which compares case, where
  the server's own lowering leaves a capital outside ASCII as it is; and the predicates were run against PostgreSQL,
  MariaDB, MySQL, SQL Server and SQL Server Compact. A text is at most 255 characters and a page at most 500 over COM
  and 1,000 over REST, and anything out of range is refused rather than cut. While the page holds only the most recent messages, its
  search asks the server a moment after the typing stops and says so - "Searched every held message on the server: 37
  match the search.", and how many match in all where more match than a page holds - keeps a check on a message only
  the answer held across the reload a release or a delete makes, and falls back to the page's own matches, saying
  why, on a failure or on a server without the search. The Deck's quarantine view does the same over REST, and its
  line says how many are held where it said how many it had listed; what a release or a delete left where it was, and
  why, and what Remove expired removed, have a line of their own under it, which stays through the reload an action
  makes and the search that reload asks again. The webmail's own list of held mail read the
  newest thousand held for anybody and kept the account's, so that on a server holding more an account's older held
  mail was never listed; it is the newest thousand held for the address now, its `total` how many are, and a search
  of it looks through every one. Like the list, a search is not on the audit trail: the quarantine is one of the
  server's working lists. `QuarantineSearchTests`, the `quarantine-search-tests` program and the `QuarantineSearch`
  and `RestApiQuarantineSearch` fixtures hold it.

- **Fixed: against a server older than the Control Panel, the Quarantine page took a method the server lacks for a
  failure.** Called through `dynamic`, as the page calls the server, a method the server does not have is the .NET
  binder's `RuntimeBinderException` ("'System.__ComObject' does not contain a definition for 'Bulk'"), never the
  COMException `DISP_E_UNKNOWNNAME` the page waited for. So on a server without `Quarantine.Bulk` a release or a delete
  stopped with that sentence where it goes one message at a time, an allow or a block did not say that the server is
  older and should be upgraded, and nor did a held message's headers or preview on a server without `ReadHeaders`.
  The page asks `ComErrorText.IsMissingMember`, which knows both; `QuarantineSearchTests` calls a COM object without
  the method to show what the binder throws, and holds that no page tells an older server by `DISP_E_UNKNOWNNAME`
  alone.

### Administration

- **Fixed: the Control Panel's IP ranges page could show no list of ranges at all (reported in work item 79), and the
  domains and rules pages cut parts of themselves off in a narrow window.** In 6.3.4 the IP ranges page's list was
  given the height the window left after the page's title, the toolbar, the permissions card and the add form, and the
  page did not scroll, so a window less than about 700 pixels high (875 at 125 % scaling) left it no room for a whole
  row, and one less than about 630 (790) no list at all: no range could be seen or selected, and so none could be
  edited or deleted. 6.3.5 kept 150 pixels of list by holding the page to the window over a fixed 560 pixels, which
  knew nothing of how tall the cards are: in the narrowest window (760 by 520), where the permissions wrap, the add
  form ran past those 560 pixels and could not be scrolled to. The page is now laid out by a new scaffold panel,
  `FillPanel`: the list takes the height the other parts leave, down to three rows, below which the whole page
  scrolls, and every other part always keeps its own height, so all of the page can be reached at every window size.
  In a narrow window the toolbar's buttons wrap where *Delete selected range* and *Restore defaults* ran off the right
  edge, the grid scrolls sideways where it squeezed the ranges' names to nothing and cut the upper address short, and
  the permissions take two columns, where a quarter of the card broke a word in two. The permissions card shows the
  selected range's permissions or none: with no range selected its boxes are clear and disabled, where they kept the
  last range's values under *Permissions (select a range)*; a save, an edit or an add keeps the range selected, where
  the reload dropped the selection and with it the card's *(saved)*; and Save, Properties and Delete find the selected
  range by its ID, where two ranges with one name and one lower address were both taken for the first of them. The
  domains and rules pages held a grid to the window over a fixed 640 and 620 pixels in the same way, and in the
  narrowest window the domains page's alias form ran past them and could not be scrolled to, its alias list had no
  height, *Create account* ran off its card and every domain's *Properties* and *Delete* off the list, and the rules
  page left a rule's actions no height and cut its match list off. Both pages are laid out by `FillPanel` now, which
  shares the window between several lists by weight: every list takes what the window leaves, down to three rows, and
  each card holds its toolbar, its list and its form whole, so all of either page can be reached at every window size.
  Below a page of 700 pixels the domains card goes above the accounts card, the alias and list cards go one above the
  other where they would be narrower than 280 pixels and the rules page's criteria and actions where they would be
  narrower than 340, *Generate* and *Create account* go under the password where they do not fit beside it, a list's
  rows are its width with a long name cut short and whole in its tool tip, and the rule grid's columns keep a width
  and scroll sideways.
- **Fixed: the Control Panel could stop answering on the rules page at some display scalings.** A list of rules,
  criteria or actions whose rows fitted only without a horizontal scroll bar, at a scaling where its columns came out a
  fraction of a pixel wider than the list, showed the horizontal bar, which left the rows too little room, so the
  vertical bar came, the columns narrowed to fit, the horizontal bar went, the rows fitted, the vertical bar went, and
  so on for ever: the page's layout never settled, and the Control Panel took no more input. In 6.3.6 four rules did it
  in a 1280 by 800 window at 175 %, and a rule with four criteria or actions in a shorter one. The criteria and actions,
  one column whose text ends in an ellipsis, no longer scroll sideways, and the list of rules, whose columns keep their
  widths and scroll sideways in a narrow window, keeps its vertical scroll bar, so that neither bar can turn the other
  on or off.
- **Fixed: the REST API's OpenAPI document described either the listing of a folder's messages or the import of a
  message into one, never both, and `GET /api/v1/status` twice.** `/api/v1/openapi.json` wrote
  `/api/v1/me/folders/{id}/messages` as two entries, one holding the `GET` and one the `POST`, since the import
  arrived on 11 September 2026, and `/api/v1/status` as two since 24 September, the second the description from
  before the event-script languages were listed in it. JSON leaves a reader to do as it likes with a member named
  twice in one object, and every reader keeps one of the two without a word: a browser's or Python's the last, so a
  client generated from the document had the import and not the listing, and the older status description; the
  server's own the first. Each path is now one entry carrying every method it answers, as the other paths with
  several were written. Nothing changed in what the server answers, only in what it says it answers.

### IMAP, POP3 and the webmail

- **The IMAP and POP3 listeners take the client's address from a PROXY protocol header, as the SMTP listener does,
  each from the peers on a list of its own.** Behind a TCP load balancer every IMAP and POP3 client had the balancer's
  address: the IP ranges, the auto-ban and an account's list of devices acted on the balancer, so that one client
  guessing passwords banned every client behind it, and a range written for one network governed all of them. Only the
  SMTP listener read the header (`TCPServer::HandleAccept`), which [ActiveActive.md](hmailserver/docs/ActiveActive.md)
  had taken for all three (unit AA-23 of its build plan). With `IMAPProxyProtocolEnabled` or `POP3ProxyProtocolEnabled`
  on and the connection's real peer on `IMAPProxyProtocolTrustedIPs` or `POP3ProxyProtocolTrustedIPs`, the connection
  must open with a version 1 or 2 header, read before an IMAPS or POP3S port's TLS handshake and before the greeting,
  and the session is the client the header names: the client's IP range is asked again, and closes the connection
  before the greeting where it would have refused the client itself; `LOGIN`, `USER`, `AUTHENTICATE`, the auto-ban,
  the devices, the logs and every event after `OnClientConnect` see the client. While a switch is on, a PROXY line
  from a peer that is not on its list closes the connection without an answer, as on SMTP - on IMAP only a line in
  the header's own form (`PROXY TCP4 `, `PROXY TCP6 `, `PROXY UNKNOWN`), since a tag is the client's to choose.
  Switched off, the default, nothing changes. The four are database settings whose rows are made at the first start
  (no schema step), on COM's `Settings` object, on `PUT /api/v1/settings` (`imap_proxy_protocol_enabled` and the
  three others) and on the IMAP and POP3 cards of the Control Panel's Protocols page. Each listener has a list of its
  own rather than SMTP's, so that a peer trusted to name SMTP clients, whom the IP ranges' relay and authentication
  rules judge, is not thereby trusted to name IMAP and POP3 ones, nor the reverse. The country policy and
  `OnClientConnect` are still asked at the accept, before the header, about the balancer, as on SMTP
  ([CountryBlocking.md](hmailserver/docs/CountryBlocking.md), [EventScripts.md](hmailserver/docs/EventScripts.md)).
  [HighAvailabilityRunbook.md](hmailserver/docs/HighAvailabilityRunbook.md) says which of a balancer's health checks
  carry the header: a check of a mail listener must, as every connection of a listed peer must, and the `/readyz`
  check of the metrics listener must not, since that listener reads no header and answers a request behind one
  `404 Not Found` (`Infrastructure.HealthProbes.AProbeBehindAProxyProtocolHeaderIsAnswered404`). In the fixtures `IMAP.ProxyProtocol` and `POP3.ProxyProtocol` (10 and 9 tests), four in each assert a refusal that
  only the named client's range or ban can give - a version 1 and a version 2 header, a range that refuses the
  protocol, and the auto-ban; the rest hold the refusal of an untrusted peer's PROXY line and of a listed peer's
  missing header, the headers that name no client, the lists kept apart, the switch off and, on IMAP, a command
  tagged PROXY. With the fix reverted 14 of the 19 fail, and the 5 that pass either way are those that assert that
  nothing changes: the switch off, the lists kept apart and the tagged command. The active-active lab's balancer
  sends `send-proxy-v2` to all three listeners, and its `proxy` scenario shows the auto-ban banning the client behind
  the balancer and not the balancer.
- **Fixed: an answer of the HTTP listeners that its handler returned after the listener's request deadline was cut off
  after its first 64 KB.** The REST API, the webmail, the Control Deck, CalDAV and CardDAV, and the web services all
  answer through one HTTP server, whose request deadline - 30 seconds on the REST listener, 15 on the web services' -
  runs while a request is read and handled. When it ran out while a handler was still working, its expiry could no
  longer be cancelled, and it closed the connection as soon as the handler's answer had handed the socket its first
  64 KB: on server1 a webmail search that took longer than thirty seconds answered 65,413 bytes of its 67,996 and was
  closed, which Python's client reported as `IncompleteRead` and the page as a search that never drew. An answer under
  64 KB arrived whole, so nothing smaller showed it. A deadline that ran out while the handler worked no longer ends
  its answer: the answer is written a piece at a time, each piece given the request deadline to be taken, as a
  download already was; the deadline is for a peer that stalls, not for an answer slow to make. A connection whose own
  deadline (five minutes after it was opened) would come first is given the time its answer needs and closed after it.
  An answer the server does end part way - a reader that stopped reading for the request deadline, the server
  stopping - now ends with a reset rather than an orderly close, which a client that does not count the bytes against
  `Content-Length` could take for the end of the answer.
- **Fixed: with the full-text index on, a webmail search on SQL Server Compact took minutes, held the database
  throughout and stalled the indexer.** Both searches - `q` on a folder's listing and `GET /api/v1/me/search` - asked
  the account's whole index before they looked at a message: every message it had read whole, then every term holding
  the word, which `LIKE '%word%'` makes every database find by reading them all. On server1, with the 100,000-message
  folder of Performance.md, one search took 75 to 180 seconds, against 0.24 s with the index off; timed on SQL Server
  Compact holding the same folder's 14 million index rows, the word's query alone took 167 seconds and the whole
  messages' 89 seconds cold. All that while the server's one SQL Server Compact connection was held, so the indexer's
  batches failed (`HM5180` after 60 seconds, then `HM6260`), and the answer came after the listener's deadline
  (above). A search now asks the index about the messages it walks past, two hundred to a query - some 40 ms on
  Compact - before it reads any of them, stops asking after about two and a half seconds and answers where to go on
  from, as it already did when its reading ran out (`complete: false`, `next_before_uid` or `next_before_id`); what
  the index leaves is read under a clock of its own. Each answer now says how many message files it opened (`opened`)
  beside how many messages it walked past (`scanned`). IMAP `SEARCH` and the eDiscovery search, which asked the whole
  account the same way at their first word, ask a window of their own messages at a time too. A row counts only as the
  indexer wrote it: a term holds a word only where the scan would find it there, and a marker only spelt as the
  indexer spells it, whatever the database's collation matches besides. On server1, with the index caught up, the
  folder's search for a word in every thousandth body answered in 5 requests of 2.5 seconds, 12.4 seconds in all, and
  IMAP `SEARCH BODY` in 12.5 seconds, with no `HM5180` while the index was built and searched; with the index off they
  take 12.5 and 9.8 seconds. On SQL Server Compact a lookup costs about what reading a small message from a fast local
  disk does, so there the index spares reads without making a search faster; it pays where reading a message is slow.
  [Performance.md](hmailserver/docs/Performance.md), "Searching".
- **Fixed: a criterion a `SEARCH`, `SORT` or `THREAD` named over and over was asked of every message as often as it
  was named, so that one command could hold an IMAP thread for the whole of `IMAPSearchTimeout`.** 6.3.6 made the `$`
  of one command - the saved search result, named a hundred thousand times in a command line - share one copy of the
  saved result, but each was still a criterion of its own, and each criterion is asked of each message: a hundred
  thousand `$` over a hundred messages were ten million questions. On server2 they took 0.44 seconds; on linix, one of
  the CI's Linux runners, the search ran out of `IMAPSearchTimeout` after 70 and then 63 of the 100 messages and was
  answered `NO [LIMIT]`, and the linux-suite job failed `SavedResultNamedOverAndOverAsASearchKeyIsAnsweredInSeconds`
  twice. The search reads the clock before each criterion, so where the clock is slow to read each question costs
  microseconds: server2, held to one core and with every clock read made 9 microseconds slower, failed the same way,
  after 64 of the 100. That reproduces linix's failure; linix's own clock was not measured. Criteria named again
  beside themselves are now left out as the command is parsed - among the command's own, every one of which a message
  must match, and between the two of an `OR` - the first staying where it stands, so that each is asked of a message
  once and every answer is what it was. The same means the same as written: the key's name in any case (`SEEN`,
  `seen`), the same `NOT`, the same value character for character, the same set, an `OR` of the same two in the same
  order. Nothing is merged that matches alike only by the key's own comparison - `SUBJECT foo` and `SUBJECT FOO`,
  `UID 1:3` and `UID 1,2,3` are both still asked - and nothing is rewritten. The hundred thousand `$` are now answered
  in 32 ms on server2, 30 ms on one core and 31 ms on one core with the slowed clock, and as the criteria of a `SORT`
  (whose slowed run had run out of the timeout too) and of a `THREAD` in 39 to 51 ms. Different criteria,
  however many, are each still asked of every message, under the same ceiling. Leaving the repeats out is one pass
  over the parsed command, and costs most where there are none to leave: a command near the largest a client can send,
  650,000 different `OR`s of two keys, is parsed in 1.2 seconds on server2 where it took 0.67 without the pass, with a
  tenth more memory at its peak. README.md's line for `IMAPSearchTimeout` said that a search which reaches it returns
  the matches found so far; it is answered `NO [LIMIT]`, with none of them.
- **Fixed: IMAP `FETCH` handed out a part's MIME header and a multipart's body written out again, not as the message
  holds them.** `BODY[N.MIME]` - and `BODY[N.HEADER]` of a part that is not a message - was each field of the part's
  header as `Name: value` with its folds undone, and `BODY[N]` of a multipart - with its `BINARY[N]` and
  `BODY[N.TEXT]` - was its parts written out again: the boundary lines spelt afresh, the epilogue dropped, and a
  closing boundary added where the message has none. So the two together were not the part `BODY[]` holds, and
  `BODY[N]` of a multipart was not as long as the part. Both are now the stored octets, folds, spacing, 8-bit bytes,
  preamble and epilogue as they are: the parse records where each part lies in the stored message, inside an
  encapsulated message too, and the sections are cut from it, read once for a message's sections and counted to their
  ceiling - from a container's original too, when the store compresses. A part whose header the parse cannot read is
  not placed, and is answered from the parse as before. `BODY[]`, `RFC822`, the message's `HEADER` and `TEXT`, a
  message/rfc822 part's body, `HEADER` and `TEXT`, and a leaf part's body already were the stored octets. Not changed:
  `HEADER.FIELDS` and `HEADER.FIELDS.NOT`, of the message or of a part, are still written out from the parsed header -
  each field's value unfolded, a field with no value left out, and for `HEADER.FIELDS` the first field of each name
  asked for, under the name as the client spelt it. And `BODYSTRUCTURE` is one a client can read where it was not: a
  message/rfc822 part whose message could take the structure past the hundred levels it describes - messages nested in
  messages, which a message of a few kilobytes can do - or whose message does not parse is described as
  `"APPLICATION" "OCTET-STREAM"` of its size, where it was a message with nothing where its body goes, or left out; a
  multipart with no parts - no boundary named, one its body never holds, one holding a NUL, which is no boundary, or
  one nested deeper than the parse descends - as the one part `FETCH` serves it as, of the size of the octets
  `BODY[N]` hands out for it, where it was a multipart with no body. A multipart whose boundary holds a NUL is now
  taken whole, as one that names none is: the boundary was searched for only as far as its NUL and no part was then
  found, so the multipart held what came before the first line beginning with that much of it, and the rest of its
  body was in neither it nor a part. `BODY`, "a form of BODYSTRUCTURE without extension data" (RFC 3501 7.4.2), no
  longer carries an attachment's disposition and file name. `IMAP/FetchPartBytes` holds `RFC822.SIZE`, `BODY[]`,
  `HEADER` with `TEXT`, every `BODYSTRUCTURE` size and line count and the octets fetched to agree, and each part to the
  octets appended, over nested multiparts, a missing closing boundary, bare line feeds, 8-bit bytes and multiparts
  with no parts, one whose boundary holds a NUL among them. `IMAPFetchPartBytesTester`, on Windows and Linux, holds
  each part's `BODY[N.MIME]`, `BODY[N]`, `BINARY[N]` of a multipart, `HEADER`, `TEXT` and partial ranges to the bytes
  written over generated messages - a quarter of them parsed from a file as the server parses a stored message, so
  read through the store - and the structures of messages nested past the depth, and of multiparts with no parts, to
  ones a client can read, the latter with the size of the octets `BODY[N]` hands out, and `BODY` to no extension data.

- **Fixed: IMAP told a user who may only drop mail into a folder its UIDVALIDITY and the UIDs it gave, let a copy or
  an append set flags the user may not set there, and left the copies a failed COPY had made.** RFC 4315 section 6
  has `APPENDUID` and `COPYUID` not given to a user who may not `SELECT` or `EXAMINE` the folder; they were given to
  anyone with the insert right. RFC 4314 section 4 has the flags a message arrives with be those the user may set in
  the folder; a copy or a move into another account's or a public folder kept `\Deleted`, `\Draft`, `\Answered`,
  `\Flagged` and the keywords whatever the rights, and an append the same but the keywords - only `\Seen` without the
  's' right was left out.
  RFC 3501 section 6.4.7 has a COPY that fails leave the destination as it was; a COPY over the quota or with a file
  that would not copy, part way through a set, left the copies already made in the destination and answered `NO`. A
  refusal by the access control is now `NO [NOPERM]` (RFC 5530), as it is meant to be told from a malformed command -
  `RENAME` without the 'x' right on the folder or the 'k' right where it would go, and `SETACL`, `GETACL` and
  `LISTRIGHTS` without the 'a' right, among them. `IMAP/CopyAndAppendRules.cs` holds each. Found by upstream's UIDPLUS
  work (upstream PRs 650 and 666), which met the same.

- **Fixed: an IMAP `COPY` or `MOVE` by message number copied or moved the wrong message when another session had just
  expunged one before it.** The server tells a session of another's expunge at the start of its next command that may
  carry an untagged `EXPUNGE`, and `COPY` and `MOVE` were such commands; but their message numbers are the ones the
  client had when it sent them, and the `EXPUNGE` renumbered the mailbox under them, so `COPY 2` copied the message
  after the one meant - or found no message of that number. The expunge is held back while a `COPY` or a `MOVE` reads
  its set, and reported in the command's own response before its `OK` - after `MOVE`'s own `EXPUNGE` - as RFC 2180
  section 4.4 has it, and before the `NO` or `BAD` of one refused before it reads its set, as before; `UID COPY` and
  `UID MOVE` name UIDs and were never at risk. A set that names the message the other session expunged - `1:*` among
  them - is now refused whole, `NO [EXPUNGEISSUED]` with the `EXPUNGE` before it, before anything is copied or moved
  (RFC 2180 section 4.4.1), so that the client sends it again in the numbering it then has, where it was read in the
  numbering the `EXPUNGE` made. `IMAP/SessionMessageNumbering.cs` copies and moves message 2 after another session
  expunged message 1, and finds the second message in the destination and the `EXPUNGE` before the `OK`, has
  `COPY 1:*` refused once and taken the second time, and finds the `EXPUNGE` before the `NO` of a `COPY` and a `MOVE`
  to a mailbox that is not there; its `COPY` test had asserted the old order. Found by upstream's UIDPLUS work
  (upstream PR 666), which holds the expunge for the next command.

- **Fixed: an IMAP session that copied messages into the folder it had selected was never told of the copies, and a
  flag change on a message another session had just added was reported before the message itself.** The server
  tells every session of a change but the one that made it, and `COPY` and `UID COPY` - unlike `APPEND` and `MOVE` -
  said nothing of their own, so the client saw neither the copies nor a count that held them until it selected the
  folder again; they are now reported with `EXISTS` and `RECENT` before the `OK`, and are the session's `\Recent` -
  but for a session that has the folder open with `EXAMINE`, which takes no message's `\Recent` (RFC 3501 6.3.2), so
  that the copies stay `\Recent` for the next session to select the folder.
  And what other sessions did was reported with the flag changes first, so a `FETCH` gave the client the number of a
  message past the end of the mailbox it knew; the `EXISTS` comes first now. `EXPUNGE` and `UID EXPUNGE`, which
  take into the session's view any message it has not been told of yet, say so with an `EXISTS` before an `EXPUNGE`
  can give one of their numbers. `IMAP/SelectedFolderReports.cs` holds the first two. Found by upstream's UIDPLUS
  work (upstream PR 666).
- **Fixed: classic Outlook for Windows, Outlook 2016 to 2024, downloaded nothing over POP3 and reported 0x800CCC90
  (reported in work item 85).** Since 6.2.0 the server's `CAPA` has listed `UTF8` (RFC 6856), and Outlook, finding it
  there, sends the `UTF8` command after `USER` and `PASS`. RFC 6856 makes `UTF8` a command of the AUTHORIZATION
  state, before the login, and the server took it there alone: after the login it was answered `-ERR Invalid command
  in current state.`, Outlook gave up there, and no mail came down, over TLS or not. Taking it after the login departs
  from the RFCs on purpose - RFC 6856 lists `UTF8` for the AUTHORIZATION state alone, and RFC 1939 has a server
  answer a command sent in the wrong state with `-ERR` - but at that point nothing has been listed or sent that the
  mode could change, so `UTF8` is now accepted after the login as well, until the session's first `STAT`, `LIST`,
  `UIDL`, `RETR`, `TOP`, `DELE` or `RSET`. After one of those it is still refused, because the mode has to hold for
  every message the session lists or sends, now with a reply that says so (`-ERR UTF8 command only valid before the
  first STAT, LIST, UIDL, RETR, TOP, DELE or RSET.`); `NOOP`, `CAPA` and `HELP` leave it open. `UTF8` before the login
  is answered as it was, and `STLS`, which a client must not send after `UTF8`, is refused after the login as it
  always was. There is no setting. IMAP has no such refusal: its `ENABLE UTF8=ACCEPT` belongs after the login
  (RFC 6855), and is accepted there. The mode still changes nothing in what is sent, a message going out as it is
  stored with `UTF8` or without, and RFC 6856's downgrade for a client that never sends `UTF8` (a surrogate message,
  or a refusal, for a message with UTF-8 in its header fields) is not done (Roadmap.md, POP3).

### Operations

- **Fixed: on Linux, a MySQL or PostgreSQL column the server reads as a `long` went through an `int` on its way
  there.** The two recordsets read such a column with `atoi`, whose `int` is narrower than Linux's 64-bit `long`, so a
  value beyond 2,147,483,647 would have come back wrong; they now read it with `strtol`, and a decimal column with
  `strtod`, the conversion `atof` made. The 64-bit ids, such as a message's, were and are read with `_atoi64`, and
  were not affected. A value in an `int`'s range reads as before, and Windows, whose `long` is an `int`'s width, reads
  every value as before. The REST API's complaints route reads its `account_id` filter with `_atoi64`, as the routes
  beside it read their ids.
- **On Linux the update check asks `rpm` whether it installed the server once in each process, through the server's
  own process launcher.** It ran `/usr/bin/rpm -q hmailserver` through `system()` and kept the answer where two
  threads asking at once could both run it; the first caller now runs it, with no shell, and the others take its
  answer. `rpm`'s standard error, which the shell line discarded, goes where the server's does.
- **Fixed: with the full-text index on, every start of the service held SQL Server Compact's one connection for
  minutes.** Before it indexed anything, the indexer removed the index rows of messages that no longer exist in one
  statement over the whole table, and again on the full-index cadence; on SQL Server Compact holding the 14 million
  rows of Performance.md's 100,000 messages that statement took 178 seconds, and on server1 the scheduled tasks that
  start with the service waited 60 seconds for the connection and failed (`HM5180`, then `HM6613` and `HM6624`), after
  the restart with the index on in both measuring runs of 7 October 2026. It now removes them a thousand message ids a
  statement, stepping over the ids the index names none of, with a pause of 50 ms between two: some 150 seconds in all
  there, no statement over 1.6 seconds. The sweep of the message metadata for the messages that are gone, which the
  indexer made at every start whether the full-text index is on or not, is cut the same way: it was one statement
  over the whole table, which a stop of the servers had to wait for (*Correctness*, above). And both now run once the
  indexer has first caught up after a start, and then on the full-index cadence, rather than before it indexes
  anything: in slices a pause apart they held back the first message by at least 50 ms for every thousand message ids
  the tables name, at every start of the service and every reinitialise, and since schema 6030 the rows they look
  for go with their message wherever foreign keys are enforced - every engine but MySQL's MyISAM - so there they
  find nothing.
- **The Windows installer gives the service's stop the minute the stop may spend on the message indexer.** Setup,
  the silent install a live update runs, and the uninstaller wait for the service to report that it has stopped for
  `ShutdownDrainSeconds` plus 30 seconds (from 6.3.4), and then refuse to go on. The service's stop now waits up to
  a minute for the indexer's thread when it is in a long statement (*Correctness*, above), so an update could be
  refused while the stop was still within that minute. The wait is now `ShutdownDrainSeconds` plus 90 seconds, and
  the wait hint the service gives the service controller for its stop says the same. Found by the re-check of the
  batch's message indexer fix.

### Build and tests

- **The Windows gate stops when the post-build step fails, where it ran the suite on the previous gate's files.**
  `build/ci/windows-gate.ps1` ran `post-build.ps1` and went on whatever it answered, so a post-build that stopped
  part-way - at a library the commit's binary manifest names and the bench has not got, as the MariaDB client's move
  to 3.4.11 under `libraries\` would have made on both benches - left the previous gate's MySQL client, type library
  and WebAdmin files beside the new server, and the gate tested those. It now ends with exit 3, `POST-BUILD FAILED`,
  and says that `get-installer-binaries.ps1` run in the bench's checkout at that commit places what is missing
  (ContinuousIntegration.md, the `windows-gate` steps). And `build/check-installer-scripts.py` holds the MySQL client
  plugins the installer names to the binary manifest's `Extras/plugin` entries both ways, with a negative control for
  each way, one for a plugin without `uninsrestartdelete` and one for the wildcard the installer took them by until
  now.

- **No tracked text file may hold a stray control character, and the seven files that did are put right.** A tool
  that reads an escape as the character it stands for writes that character where the escape was meant to go, and
  nothing on the screen shows it. `hmailserver/docs/RegressionEnvironment.md` said `installation\Extras`, a BEL and
  `za.exe`, its `\7` taken for an octal escape, and the help page the server serves from it carried the BEL;
  `build/check-cli.py`'s pattern for a colour code began with a raw ESC where `\x1b` was written; and four C# tests -
  two XOAUTH2 strings, `AttachmentTextSearch`'s binary attachment and a label `ApiKeyStore.ValidateLabel` refuses -
  held SOH, STX, ETX, EOT and DEL raw. Those were the values meant, and they are now written as four-digit escapes,
  since C#'s `\x` takes up to four hex digits: `"\x01auth"` is U+001A followed by `uth`. `MessageIndexing.cs` had a
  line ending CR CR LF, which also kept git from normalising that file's line ends. `build/check-control-bytes.py`
  now refuses, in every tracked text file, a C0 control character other than tab, line feed and carriage return,
  DEL, and a carriage return not followed by a line feed. The five files that hold one on purpose - the LGPL text's
  form feeds, the NUL that ends three RTF licences, and the CR CR LF inside an SQL Server Compact upgrade script's
  message - are listed with their reasons, and the check proves its own negative controls on every run; the
  *checkers* job runs it with every other `build/check-*.py`.

- **UTS 46 is held to Unicode's conformance tests on both platforms, and to a browser's URL parser by a differential
  fuzz.** `idna-tests`, a new tester program, runs `IdnaTester` on Linux - every line of `IdnaTestV2.txt` 18.0.0 four
  ways, and Punycode, NFC and the URL standard's domain parser - in `linux-build`, and the source packages'
  `dh_auto_test` and `%check` run it with the other testers; on Windows it runs in ClassTester. Its tables and test
  lines are generated by `build/generate-idna-tables.py` from the six Unicode 18.0.0 files under `Common/Idna/ucd`, each
  held to its SHA-256; `checkers` runs it with `--check` beside the other generators, and SonarQube Cloud's scope leaves
  its two files out, as it does theirs (`.sonarcloud.properties`); the data's Unicode License v3 is in
  `hmailserver/docs/Licenses/`, the packages' copyright file, the Windows installer's licence, the source tarball's
  required files and the SBOM. So are the BSD 3-Clause terms of HTML's list of named character references - the
  standard's terms for a portion of it incorporated into source code - whose table `build/generate-html-references.py`
  writes from the standard's own `entities.json`, held to its SHA-256 likewise and run with `--check` in `checkers`.
  `build/ci/idna-differential-fuzz.sh` builds the server's core library with libFuzzer and AddressSanitizer beside ada
  4.0.0, the URL parser of Node.js, taken from PyPI and Unicode's files from unicode.org, each pinned, nothing from
  GitHub, and puts every input to the domain parser, `SURBL::HostOfAuthority` and the link reader in text and in HTML -
  once as written and once in character references, every code point past ASCII that has a named reference written as
  one - on both sides, and holds the link reader to handing over every host 6.3.6 handed over for the input, by a copy
  of 6.3.6's reading (`fuzz/harness/surbl_636_reading.h`), whatever ada makes of it, and to handing over ada's host when
  the input is followed by a closing quotation mark, in text and as `&rdquo;` in HTML's text, or by an ideographic full
  stop and CJK, wherever the server's rule puts a place a mail program may end the link at there; before it fuzzes it
  holds the server's NFC to `NormalizationTest.txt` and ada to `IdnaTestV2.txt`, so that what it sets aside - the code
  points whose Unicode tables differ between the two, and ada's four departures from UTS 46 (its joiner and bidi rules,
  a name it leaves out of NFC, and Punycode that begins with its delimiter) - is shown to be the tables' or ada's,
  against Unicode's own files, RFC 3492 and ada's own label check. The one defect of the server's it found before
  release is kept in `fuzz/regression/idna_ada_fuzzer` and replayed before every run fuzzes, beside an input of ada's
  joiner departure in a label written `xn--`, which the rule for it now covers, and one of a symbol percent-encoded
  before a name and a quotation mark after it, which a mail program sees as ASCII. Its 30-minute run on server2 on the
  night of 12 October 2026, from a fresh build: no difference in 1,819 seconds, about 47.9 million inputs; and on 13
  October 2026, with the two checks above, from the corpus the runs before had left: no difference in 1,807 seconds,
  about 36.4 million inputs in 159 jobs, none of them a crash or a timeout under AddressSanitizer, and 10,228 inputs in
  the corpus at the end; and after the second check's repairs, with the check of where a mail program ends a link: no
  difference in 1,807 seconds, about 39.9 million inputs in 160 jobs, none a crash or a timeout
  ([Fuzzing.md](hmailserver/docs/Fuzzing.md), "UTS 46 against ada").
- **Fixed: the database matrix laid the server's tree out where a command run beside the server as root is refused,
  so that its whole suite failed one test on every engine.** A command run as root runs on as root only over folders
  no other account could have put a symbolic link in ([ServiceAccount.md](hmailserver/docs/ServiceAccount.md), "On
  Linux, a command run as root"), and `build/ci/linux-suite.sh` lays its tree out inside the checkout only when the
  way to the checkout is root's alone, and in `/var/lib/hmtest-tree` in the job's container when it is not.
  `build/lab/db-suite.sh`, which the `db-matrix` job and `build/lab/lab.sh suite` run, laid it out inside the checkout
  always - which GitLab's docker executor makes under umask 0000 and a lab's `docker run -v` mounts as its user's - so
  that with `HM_SUITE_FILTER=all` `hmailserver --apply-environment` refused the tree (exit 2) and
  `AutoBanHookRetry.ACommandRunBesideTheServerLeavesWhatIsBelowItAlone` failed; the database-sensitive fixtures, its
  default, do not hold that test. It now chooses as `linux-suite.sh` does, and makes the tree under umask 0022. Found
  by the whole suite on MySQL 8.4, MariaDB 11.8 and PostgreSQL 17 at the fold of active-active's landing B1, where it
  was the one failure on each engine.
- **The database layer counts the rows a statement matched, on all four backends, and has the database's clock in UTC:
  the first unit of active-active (AA-01 in ActiveActive.md), which nothing in the server uses yet.**
  `DatabaseConnectionManager::ExecuteCount` runs a statement as `Execute` does - the same fault injection, measuring
  and audit - and answers the rows it matched, or -1 when it failed, and whether the connection was lost while it ran,
  after which the layer runs it again: ADO's `RecordsAffected` on SQL Server and SQL Server Compact,
  `mysql_affected_rows` on MySQL and MariaDB, now connected with `CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS` so that an update which sets what
  a row already holds counts the row as the other engines do, and `PQcmdTuples` on PostgreSQL. SQL Server's sessions
  are opened with `NOCOUNT` off, as a session is unless the server's `user options` turn it on, since under it there
  is no count. `SQLStatement::GetCurrentUtcTimestamp` and `GetCurrentUtcTimestampPlusSeconds` give `SYSUTCDATETIME()`,
  `UTC_TIMESTAMP(6)` and PostgreSQL's `statement_timestamp() at time zone 'utc'` - the statement's time, not the
  transaction's, which `now()` is - and on SQL Server Compact, which has no UTC function (its provider refuses all
  four it might have), the node's own UTC clock. `DatabaseClaimTester` holds them on a real database through the
  server's own connections: in the Windows suite's internal tests on a SQL Server Compact database of its own, and as
  `database-claim-tests`, which `linux-build` makes beside the server and the Linux suite and the database matrix run
  against their PostgreSQL, MySQL or MariaDB before the server starts (it says SKIPPED with no database) - the counts,
  a claim run again as a reconnect runs it, two connections racing for the same rows and for named leases that have no
  row yet, a connection closed, ended and timed out under a claim, a lease on the UTC clock refused, renewed, taken
  and fenced, and the UTC clock against the machine's. On SQL Server 2022 the same checks held inside the server,
  through `ADOConnection`, on a node of the active-active lab's Windows half; with the server's `user options` turning
  `NOCOUNT` on, a build without the `NOCOUNT` statement counted -1 there and this one did not. The lab's engine checks
  (`build/lab/active-active/sqlcheck.py`) gained the same claim run twice, named leases, SQL Server at READ
  UNCOMMITTED with writers that roll back - where a reader saw rows that were then rolled back, and with the
  `READCOMMITTED` hint none - and a lease on the local wall clock and one on the UTC clock across both daylight-saving
  changes, on a database in `Europe/London` whose clock libfaketime moves (`aa-lab.sh up-dst` and `dst`): on
  PostgreSQL, MariaDB and MySQL the wall-clock lease was taken an hour early in spring and held an hour late in
  autumn, the UTC one neither. A unit runs a lab of its own with `AA_PREFIX` and `AA_HOME`.

- **Every change is checked before it lands, a maintainer's batch as well as a merge request** (OpenSSF Baseline
  OSPS-VM-05.03 and OSPS-VM-06.02). `semgrep-sast`, `semgrep-sast-gate` and `mr-dependency-check` ran in a merge
  request's pipeline alone, and a maintainer's `batch*` branch, whose merge request runs no pipeline of its own, landed
  without them - 6.3.5's and 6.3.6's batches among them. They now run in a protected `batch*` branch's pipeline too, the
  one GitLab holds its merge request to, judged against where the batch leaves `master` (`change_base()` in
  `build/ci/security-gate.py`; `--merge-request auto`, `--base auto`): blocking, with no `rules:changes` list, no rule
  that reads `SAST_DISABLED`, and tried twice more when an input cannot be read (exit 2) or GitLab itself fails.
  `semgrep-sast` runs GitLab's analyzer from a copy in the project's registry that keeps its digest
  (`mirror/semgrep`, made by `build/ci/mirror-semgrep.sh`): on 5 October 2026 GitLab's registry stopped serving the
  digest pinned on 26 September, which would now have stopped every change. On a batch, `static-analysis`, `semgrep`,
  `ci-image-packages` and `dependency-scan` compare the branch with `master` rather than with the push before, so a
  push of documentation on top of code still runs them. `build/land-via-mr.py` lands a batch only when each gate in
  its pipeline succeeded itself - the three change checks always, the two source scans unless the batch changes
  Markdown alone at the root or under a dot-directory - since GitLab calls a pipeline a success with a job a rule left
  out or one that failed while allowed to, and it writes their statuses into the landing record.
  `build/check-release-chain.py` holds all of it, each rule with a case of its self-test that must fail
  (SECURITY.md, "Every change"; ContinuousIntegration.md, "Change checks"). And `.own-runners`' paths name the
  files called `d` and `md`, which their patterns left out, so that a change to one runs the project's runners'
  jobs as a change to any file that is not a document does.
- **A change cannot silence its own finding.** `semgrep-sast-gate` holds a change that adds an entry to
  `build/ci/static-analysis-baseline.txt` or `build/ci/semgrep-baseline.txt`, or takes a reason from one, and one that
  raises, in any file a scan reads, the count of the inline comments by which Semgrep, clang-tidy or cppcheck passes
  over a finding; a change may delete an entry, or give one its reason. A change that alters the scan's configuration
  answers for every finding in the tree, as before, and now so does one that removes or moves one of its files, which
  the gate read as touching nothing. When it re-pins the analyzer, and only then, its own copy of the exceptions file
  may accept a finding in a file it does not touch, never in one it does, so that re-pinning a vanished analyzer need
  not wait on an exception no gate could judge.
- **A narrowing of what a scan reads lands alone, as a declaration.** Whole-tree mode widens what counts and cannot
  see a finding a change keeps out of the report: a `.semgrepignore` (GitLab's analyzer includes the root's), an entry
  of `SAST_EXCLUDED_PATHS` or `SAST_SEMGREP_EXCLUDED_PATHS` in any CI file, the analyzer's options, a custom ruleset,
  the source scans' ignore and suppression lists - a line gained, or a `!` line Semgrep's list loses or puts before the
  line it takes back from - clang-tidy's checks, or the lines of `static-analysis.sh` and `semgrep.sh` that choose what
  cppcheck, clang-tidy and Semgrep read and report (the files, options and checks, the rules each pack brings, and
  what of a failed run stands as the report), now marked `# scan-scope begin` and `# scan-scope end`, or one of
  those tools' options put outside them, could hide the finding the same change brought. `semgrep-sast-gate`
  holds a change that narrows what a scan reads while it changes anything else a scan reads; a narrowing that lands
  by itself, with its documents, passes. `static-analysis.sh` refuses `HM_TIDY_CHECKS` in a GitLab job, so that no
  project variable chooses its checks, and `semgrep.sh` refuses to run without its ignore list, without which Semgrep's
  default would leave out `build/` and every test directory. `semgrep-sast`'s exclusions are held to the root -
  Semgrep's `--exclude` and GitLab's report filter read `tests` as any directory of that name, as the analyzer's
  Semgrep 1.174 showed on 6 October 2026 - and the job sets `SAST_SEMGREP_EXCLUDED_PATHS` to nothing itself. A source
  file moved to where the scan does not read it - as git pairs a move, or deleted while a file of its name is added
  there, a move rewritten past what git pairs - or added under a `vendor/`, `dist/` or `build/` below the root, which
  the analyzer's own template leaves out, is held too. SECURITY.md says that the scripts under `build/`, the gates'
  own among them, are read by the `semgrep` job alone, in a batch, and that an edit of the vendored zlib or QuickJS
  sources is read by no gate.
- **A report the scan did not write in this pipeline stands for nothing.** `semgrep-sast` was `allow_failure`, so a
  scan that failed - an image the registry no longer served, a timeout - let `semgrep-sast-gate` run on whatever
  `gl-sast-report.json` the checkout held, a committed one among them. `semgrep-sast` is no longer `allow_failure`, and
  removes `gl-sast-report.json` and `semgrep.sarif` before its analyzer runs; the gate, and the release job, refuse a
  tree that tracks a scan's report, and a `semgrep-sast` report that GitLab's analyzer did not write or that began
  before the pipeline was created; `.gitignore` keeps the scans' outputs out of a `git add`. `semgrep-sast` keeps
  Semgrep's SARIF beside its report, and the gate holds a change to a file one of Semgrep's rules gave up on, which the
  analyzer leaves at a warning. It reads the SARIF in the words of the analyzer it was checked against (6.26.1,
  Semgrep 1.174.0, kept word for word in its self-test): a notification of a kind it does not know, a time limit that
  names no file of the checkout as the analyzer names one (from the root: a `./` or an absolute path would match no
  changed file), or a SARIF with no run stops it as an input it cannot read (exit 2), never a pass, and its
  self-test fails while `semgrep-sast` pins another analyzer, until the new one's words are read
  (`build/ci/mirror-semgrep.sh`'s header; ContinuousIntegration.md, "Re-pinning `semgrep-sast`'s analyzer").
- **A fork's merge request runs a pipeline of its own, and does not land on it.** The workflow's first rule compared a
  merge request's source project with `CI_PROJECT_ID`, which in a fork's pipeline is the fork's, so a merge request from
  a fork's protected branch ran no merge request pipeline and was held to a branch pipeline that runs no gate. The rule
  now leaves a merge request without a pipeline of its own only when it comes from a protected `batch*` branch of this
  project, and `build/check-release-chain.py` holds it to the branches the gates run for. A fork's pipeline runs on
  runners its owner chooses, so SECURITY.md says a fork's change lands through a batch, or on a pipeline run here, and
  `build/land-via-mr.py` refuses a pipeline another project ran.
- **The gates' base is GitLab's, and the landing reads it back.** A variable a CI file defines stands in for GitLab's
  own, so a change could name its own base. `change_base()` takes `CI_MERGE_REQUEST_DIFF_BASE_SHA` only in a merge
  request's pipeline, and only when it is an ancestor of the head and of the target branch; a CI file that defines a
  `CI_*` or `GITLAB_*` variable holds the change, and `check-release-chain.py` refuses one; and `land-via-mr.py` reads
  "The base:" from each gate's log and refuses a landing whose gates judged it against anything but `master`'s tip.
- **A change to the gates' own code is judged by the base's copy too.** The gates ran the change's own scripts, so an
  edit of them judged the change that made it. When a change alters `security-gate.py`, `security-findings.py`,
  `mr-dependency-check.py`, `dependency-scan.py` or `osv-offline-db.py`, each gate also runs the base's copies over a
  worktree of the change's head, and a hold from either holds it. Whether the base's copy runs is read from the code
  that runs, against the base's, never from a variable, so neither a CI file nor a project variable can stop it; each
  gate says in its log how the copy ended, and `land-via-mr.py` lands a batch that changes the gates' code only when
  both logs say it passed. Each script of the gates and of the landing takes its own directory off Python's module
  path before it imports anything else, so that a `build/ci/json.py` a change adds does not run as the gate's `json`.
  `land-via-mr.py` lands a batch that changes the gates' own files - their code, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, the CI files the
  gate jobs are in or take a part from (`mr-checks.yml`, `gitlab-security.yml`, `no-github.yml`), itself,
  `check-release-chain.py`, `sign-off.py` and `scan-secrets.py`, which it runs, and the source scans' scripts,
  `static-analysis.sh` and `semgrep.sh` - only with `--gates-read "<reason>"`, a person's word that the change was
  read, which the landing record keeps (exit 9 without it), and only when `checkers` succeeded itself;
  `check-release-chain.py` holds that list to the files the gate jobs reach with `extends` and `!reference`, refuses a
  second definition, in another CI file, of a job that holds a change or of a template one reaches - GitLab merges
  the two, a later include's keys over an earlier one's - and a CI file but `.gitlab-ci.yml` that sets `variables`,
  `default` or `workflow` or includes anything but GitLab's templates, and holds each Python script of the list to
  the line that keeps its directory off the module path. SECURITY.md says the gates stand against mistakes, not
  against a change that edits the jobs themselves.
- **`mr-dependency-check` holds a requirement that pins no version, and does not take OSV's silence for an answer.** A
  requirements line it could not read as `name==version` - a range, `name @ <url>`, another index - was skipped; one a
  change adds now holds it, and so does a `-r` or `-c` naming a requirements file the tree does not hold (a URL, an
  absolute path) and a `${...}` pip takes from the environment. A control that OSV is known to name (OpenSSL's, Boost's, zlib's, Connector/C's, 7-Zip's)
  that draws no advisory is OSV's data not read, exit 2, and `dependency-scan` fails its scan for it; a version older
  than its control that OSV names nothing for, while it names the control's, is held by the control's advisories as
  ones that may affect it (OpenSSL 0.9.6 draws none, 4.0.0 43). A base whose lock file or exceptions file cannot be
  read, or whose exceptions file has an entry reviewed after today, holds no change by that alone - the file names
  or accepts nothing - so that the change that mends it can land.
- **`static-analysis` and `semgrep` pass a finding that `master`'s exceptions file accepts, and their baselines only
  shrink.** A finding new to a baseline failed the job unless the baseline took it, which needed no reason, reviewer or
  expiry and was read from the change itself. Each job now reads `master`'s `.gitlab/security-exceptions.yml` -
  `static-analysis` with git, which it installs with its tools, `semgrep` from the project's API - through
  `security-gate.py`'s own reader, passes a new finding that an exception in force accepts, and fails (exit 2) when
  the file cannot be read; an exception within 30 days of its expiry is named in the log. `--write-baseline` keeps the
  entries still found, drops those gone and adds none, and `--reasons` gives a reason only to an entry that has none.
  The artifacts gain `accepted-findings.txt` and `master-security-exceptions.yml`.
- **The eight High baseline entries that had no reason have one.** Six of Semgrep's parse the project's own
  catalogues, a nuspec rendered from its template or a TRX the suite wrote, or start node with an argument list;
  `hmctl`'s unverified TLS context is made only for `--insecure` to a loopback address; and `CrashSimulation.cpp`'s
  null write is the crash handler's deliberate test, reached only through a setting a server administrator sets. None
  was fixed: the XML rule accepts only `defusedxml`, which the checkers job does not install, and the crash tests need
  the fault. 475 of `static-analysis`'s 691 entries and 62 of `semgrep`'s 125 have no reason yet; they are triaged by
  31 March 2027.
- **`mr-dependency-check` asks about the native and vendored libraries, and honours the VEX document.** A change that
  moved the pin of OpenSSL, Boost, libpq, zlib, QuickJS, MariaDB Connector/C, 7-Zip or SQL Server Compact was listed
  as not checked; each new version is now asked of `api.osv.dev` by its upstream tag, with a control version beside it
  as `dependency-scan` asks, and held on a Critical or High advisory. One older than its repository's first tag is
  held by that tag's advisories, and a library OSV has no usable data for is listed as UNKNOWN. A Critical or High
  advisory now passes when the base's VEX document declares the package at that version not affected, matched by
  purl, as well as when the base's exceptions accept it. Its self-test holds zlib 1.2.11 on CVE-2022-37434.
- **`dependency-scan` rates an advisory that carries only a CVSS 4.0 vector, and dismisses one only for the version a
  VEX statement names.** It read CVSS 3.x vectors and database ratings alone, so CVE-2026-76844, in zlib's
  `gz_write`, which its CVSS 4.0 vector rates 8.3, High, with a fixed version, counted as Unknown; it is now scored by
  `mr-dependency-check.py`'s calculator, and would hold the release. The VEX document says zlib 1.3.2 is not affected:
  `gzwrite.c` is not vendored. A VEX statement dismissed an advisory for any version of the library; it now needs the
  library at the version scanned among its products, by purl. Its new `--self-test` runs in `checkers`.
- **`dependency-scan`'s line for the CI image counts the kernel headers apart.** Of the image's 3,608 advisories on 6
  October 2026, 3,535 were against `linux-libc-dev`, the kernel's user-space headers, which hold no kernel code:
  Trivy files every advisory against the kernel's source package under it. The CI image's test case now counts those
  apart from the 73 against the image's other packages, each by severity. Every advisory stays in the reports and
  `findings.txt` (and, since the next entry, one against the headers that has a fixed version is not affected).
- **`dependency-scan` and the release gate treat `linux-libc-dev` as a header-only package, whose advisories are
  not affected.** Ubuntu published `linux-libc-dev` 7.0.0-38.38, and `batch44`'s pipeline 2924313539 (8 October
  2026) counted 60 kernel advisories against the CI image's 7.0.0-34.34 headers as High or Critical with a fixed
  version (3,610 in all, 15 dismissed by the VEX document), on which the release gate would have held the next
  release: headers that hold no kernel code, in an image that holds no kernel, under which Trivy files every advisory
  against the kernel's source package. The new rule `HEADER_ONLY` in `build/ci/dependency-scan.py` names the image's
  header-only packages, that one today, with the reason: an advisory against one of them in the CI image's scan is
  listed in every report with the status "not affected: header-only package, the advisory is against the kernel it
  was built from" - the GitLab report's record carries it in its `details`, under the record's own id, so the
  dashboard shows it - and counted apart in the image's test case, and it is never among the high or critical with a
  fixed version, by the scan or by `build/ci/security-gate.py`, which reads the same rule off the record's package and
  location and says in the release job's log what it spared. The rule reaches that name alone, and the image's scan
  alone: a High with a fixed version against any other package, or against the same name in a lock file, counts as
  before; both self-tests hold it ([SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md), "Dependencies").
- **`build/ci/mirror-semgrep.sh` and `build/ci/mirror-tumbleweed.sh` handle no token.** `mirror-tumbleweed.sh` read a
  registry token from its standard input for `skopeo login`, and `repo-hygiene`'s Token-Permissions check failed on it,
  in `batch43`'s pipeline 2916285454, as a script that reads a token where no job runs it. Both now take a
  `docker login registry.gitlab.com` made before they run, best in a `DOCKER_CONFIG` of its own, and hand the file it
  wrote to skopeo, read-only and for the copy's destination alone; they refuse a login kept in a credential helper,
  which skopeo's container cannot reach. Token-Permissions no longer fails on either.
- **The DNSSEC validator is tested against answers captured from the public DNS** (work item 80).
  `DnssecResolverTester`, which the service's class tests run on Windows and `dane-tests` on Linux, now runs the
  resolver on its own thread against replies captured on 7 October 2026 (`DnssecCapturedAnswers.h`), with its clock
  at their capture and the built-in root anchors: live.com's and cloudflare.com's MX RRsets validate from the root's
  keys down, debian.org's under both its RSA/SHA-256 and ECDSA P-256 signatures, and the same answers expired,
  altered - the exchange, the signature, the key tag it names, the key-signing key the DS record names, an MX record
  added - and stripped of their signatures fail with the reason the log gives, while the signed record repeated in
  another spelling is counted once - nothing is sent, and the tester's answers reach no other thread and no cache. It
  also holds the canonical form itself: an exchange compressed and in mixed case is written out and lowercased, and
  a pointer that points at itself or forwards, or a name that runs past its RDATA, is refused. The suite's DNS server
  now sends an MX record's exchange compressed against the question, as resolvers do, so every signed delivery in
  `SMTP/DaneIndeterminateLookups` goes through it, with a test of an exchange in mixed case besides;
  `Security/DnssecCompressedMx` (Windows) holds the verdicts and the debug log's reason.
- **The static-analysis job's baseline holds 691 findings, down from 887.** The 191 that the security dashboard's
  triage of 5 October 2026 marked to harden or fix are changed in the code, and five more went with the same edits:
  the Linux command line's and `openpgp-writer`'s unchecked writes to the terminal discard their results with
  `(void)`, members and locals take their value where they are declared, the REST handlers' assignments leave their
  `if` conditions, branches with one body are joined, `StdString.h`'s SSMIN and SSMAX return by value, its no-op
  statements are cast to `(void)` and FmtArg's assignment is deleted, `IMAPResult`'s assignment checks for
  self-assignment, the ini file's and the file-backed settings' whole-file read loops stop at the first short read,
  two static-only classes' private destructors are no longer virtual, the LDAP client's option pointer and the
  recipient callout's read buffer say in so many words what they hold, the PST reader's child sets its signal mask
  with `pthread_sigmask`, three widening casts widen before the arithmetic, and six of the seven sites cppcheck rated
  High read as its model follows them (the seventh, CrashSimulation.cpp's null pointer, is deliberate and stays).
  Apart from the two entries under Operations, none of them changes what the server does. `openpgp-writer`, a test
  tool, now ends with 1, saying why, when its message could not be written to standard output, where it ended with 0.
- **The testers' four timing checks of computation that 6.3.6 left out take `HM_TEST_TIME_BOUND` as well**, ten times
  their margin where the aarch64 RPM builds run them under qemu-user: ImipTester's three fixed margins (a quarter of a
  second, 0.02 s, a quarter of a second) over the expansions they are measured against, and XmlDocument's 3000 ms for
  its worst-case document. The 6.3.6 tag's `rpm-fedora43-aarch64` failed once on the 0.02 s margin (0.1547 s against
  0.1424 s). The checks that race a real sleep or a deadline - NeverBanNameList's two and `network-deadline-tests`' -
  keep their bounds: emulation does not slow a sleep, and ten times theirs would pass a deadline that was not kept.
- **The Tumbleweed RPM jobs take their images from the project's own registry.** openSUSE's registry drops a rolling
  snapshot within weeks: the x86_64 image 6.3.6 was built in (`bc34ab33…`) answered 404 on 6 October 2026, so a
  pipeline on a runner without it cached could not have started those jobs. The 6 October snapshot's linux/amd64 and
  linux/arm64 images are copied, digests preserved, to
  `registry.gitlab.com/hmailserver/hmailserver/mirror/opensuse-tumbleweed`, which `.gitlab/ci/packages-rpm.yml` now
  pins; `build/ci/mirror-tumbleweed.sh` takes a new snapshot when one is wanted, and Renovate leaves the pins alone.
  Both packages build in it (clang 23.1.2, the rest as before), every tester passing - the aarch64 one's under
  qemu-user - and each installs in its architecture's image and answers `--version`.
- **The Linux jobs run on the CI image as the project's registry holds it, named by the digest of its manifest, and
  each starts by checking that it was started so.** `.linix` named `hmailserver-ci/linux:26.04-52e9976e73bf`, which
  each runner with the tag `linix` found in its own image store and never pulled: a tag is only a name, and a job that
  is root on linix in effect - the privileged `linix-systemd` entry's - could have given it other bytes, which every
  later job, a release's packages among them, would then have built in (the second security review of 6.3.6,
  SUP2-1). On 6 October 2026 the image was pushed with `build/ci/build-linux-image.sh --push` to
  `registry.gitlab.com/hmailserver/hmailserver/ci-linux`, which anyone can pull from, and `.linix` now names it
  `ci-linux:26.04-52e9976e73bf@sha256:4eead001…`: Docker takes an image named so only as the registry holds that
  digest, and linix and server2 both pull it from there. `.linix`'s `before_script` is
  `python3 build/check-ci-image.py --job`, and `container-image-sbom`, `container-image-start` and
  `container-image-start-arm64`, which take its image without extending it, start with the same step: it stops the
  job before it builds anything unless the image it was started in is named so, with the tag of the commit's own
  Dockerfile. The registry's cleanup policy, still switched off, keeps this image's tags and the Tumbleweed mirror's
  by name since the same day.
- **The CI image was rebuilt on 8 October 2026, from the unchanged Dockerfile, for Ubuntu's kernel-header and libc
  updates.** The image pushed on 6 October carried `linux-libc-dev` 7.0.0-34.34; Ubuntu then published 7.0.0-38.38,
  and `dependency-scan` in `batch44`'s pipeline counted 60 kernel advisories against the headers as High or Critical
  with a fixed version, which would have held the next release. The rebuild carries `linux-libc-dev` 7.0.0-38.38,
  `libc6` 2.43-2ubuntu2.4 and `openssl` 3.5.5-1ubuntu3.7, and `.linix` names it
  `ci-linux:26.04-52e9976e73bf@sha256:35048402…`. The rule for a rebuild at the same Dockerfile: it builds to the same
  tag, `26.04-<hash>`, and `build/ci/build-linux-image.sh --push` moves that tag in the registry to the new image's
  digest; the pin in `.linix` follows the digest, in a commit of its own, with `build/check-ci-image.py` holding the
